articles.title: The Sample Passed. What Did We Actually Prove?
articles.excerpt: Why a clean control test can still leave a decision maker exposed By Manfredi Marrocco The report says every sampled access removal was completed on time. The dashboard turns green. A manager asks whe…
articles.body: Why a clean control test can still leave a decision maker exposed By Manfredi Marrocco The report says every sampled access removal was completed on time. The dashboard turns green. A manager asks whether the company can now rely on its leaver process. There is a missing question: did the sample come from a complete list of leavers? If the test began with tickets already created in the identity system, it may have excluded precisely the cases where nobody created a ticket. Ten well-processed tickets can demonstrate that those ten tickets were well processed. They cannot, by themselves, establish that all departures entered the process, or that the same process worked in every subsidiary. This distinction has practical consequences.

articles.title: Game Analytics: The Events Every Mobile Game Should Track
articles.excerpt: The short answer Track a small, planned set of events in six groups: sessions, the first-launch funnel, progression, economy, monetization and technical health. Write them in a tracking plan before co…
articles.body: The short answer Track a small, planned set of events in six groups: sessions, the first-launch funnel, progression, economy, monetization and technical health. Write them in a tracking plan before coding, name them consistently and attach parameters. With about twenty well-chosen events you can calculate retention, find where players quit, balance the economy and see why revenue rises or falls. Start from questions Events exist to answer questions. Write the questions first. Where do new players drop out in the first ten minutes? Which level is too hard? Are players running out of currency or sitting on piles of it? Which ad placement is used most? Do players who use a feature stay longer? Is the game stable on low-end phones? If an event answers none of your questions, do not add it.

articles.title: The Future of Micro-Frontends: How to Combine Module Federation with Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
articles.excerpt: Client-side Module Federation has a well-known weakness, the browser downloads a shell, then fetches remotes, then renders. Users stare at a blank page, and crawlers may see very little. For content-h…
articles.body: Client-side Module Federation has a well-known weakness, the browser downloads a shell, then fetches remotes, then renders. Users stare at a blank page, and crawlers may see very little. For content-heavy or SEO-sensitive products, that's a deal-breaker, and it's why teams keep asking the same question, can we get independently deployed micro-frontends **and * server-rendered HTML?* The answer is yes, with caveats. Module Federation supports server-side rendering, and the same model that works in the browser transfers to Node, a host fetches code from remotes at runtime and renders it on the server. But SSR raises the stakes. You now have two runtimes to keep consistent, a network dependency inside your render path, and a security boundary you didn't have before.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

The fledgling Xbox console was not quite a year old, and when I got settled in on the staff, it quickly became clear that Xbox was really about one thing above all else: Halo. I remember being surprised in my first days on the job by what would happen every single day, like clockwork, at 5pm: consoles and TVs would get turned on, Halo would get fired up, and we’d all play a round or two of Capture the Flag on Blood Gulch before we all went home. articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

articles.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
articles.excerpt: SpaceX just made spaceflight history, catching the upper stage of its Starship megarocket when it returned to Earth. But Starship still has some pretty big boxes left to check.
articles.body: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off. articles.body: After aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15's booster, SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its "Mechazilla" launch and catch tower for the first time. The company has performed ' chopstick ' catches of its boosters before, but this is the first time the maneuver has successfully been executed on the Starship vehicle itself.
